title: Research on the Construction of Aerobic Biological Treatment Systems for Coal Chemical Wastewater and Mechanisms for System Collapse Recovery
description: Coal chemical wastewater (CCW) is rich in intricate aromatic compounds, causing instability in the biochemical treatment system, potentially resulting in system failure. This study extensively investigates strategies and mechanisms for restoring aerobic biochemical treatment systems on the brink of collapse. Findings reveal that with influent COD concentration at 2052.69 mg/L and the ammonium nitrogen (NH4+-N) concentration at 304.08 mg/L, removal rates are 30.23% and 45.06%, respectively, indicating the collapse of the aerobic biochemical treatment system at this juncture.After a 30-day incubation period with Acinetobacter pittii, COD removal rate reached 83.91%, and NH4+-N removal rate reached 71.65%. This indicated that the system had achieved the treatment level prior to its collapse, showcasing the significant reparative impact of introducing this strain. Subsequent analysis delved into the repair mechanism of the system, revealing a shift towards aromatic compound-degrading bacteria such as Pseudomonas, Thauera, Acinetobacter, and Comamonas as the dominant genera, accompanied by notable increases in PN and PS contents. The alpha-helix/(beta-folding + random coil) ratio increased gradually to 0.42 (LB-EPS) and 0.39 (TB-EPS) over the repair process. Microbial metabolic regulation analysis highlighted the upregulation of key enzymes including DHA, C12O, and C23O. This upregulation was mirrored in enzymes such as catechol 1,2-dioxygenase, catechol 2,3-dioxygenase, protocatechuate 3,4-dioxygenase, and protocatechuate 4,5-dioxygenase, demonstrating enhanced expression of relevant original enzyme genes. These findings underscore the substantial positive impact of functional strain enhancement on system repair.
